BULGARIAN MAFIA

By: Marion Edmunds | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight we reveal how the Bulgarian Mafia put down it's roots in Cape Town creating criminal networks which have led to drug smuggling, human trafficking and murders...neither friend or enemy are spar

Unique Selling Point:
The murder of four Bulgarian nationals in Constantia on May 25th gives us a hook on which to build the complex story of the Bulgarian Mafia in Cape Town and how poor policing, dodgy immigration lawyers and an unprotected coastline facilitated the flourishing of a violent criminal group, often in the shadows of quiet suburbs.

Summary:
In South Africa life is cheap. Despite this, it’s an attractive destination for foreign criminals building global trade routes, who can exploit the Cape's rugged unprotected coastline and faltering police services for their own nefarious ends.



On the 25th of May this year, a wet Thursday morning, four Bulgarian nationals were shot dead in their home in Constantia just after 08h00 am. The main target it appears was fifty-five-year-old KRASIMIR NIKOLAEV KAMENOV, a Bulgarian wanted by Interpol on behalf of the Bulgarian Police. But the assassins also took out his wife, their au pair and one of their two bodyguards, leaving three orphaned children.



The South African Police moved swiftly to close up the broken entrance and comb the large house for clues, seizing ADT footage from the cameras that watch the street. It’s a high profile case which was scooped up by the Hawks, who have yet to formally identify the victims.



Kamanev’s neighbours, who rarely saw him and the family, were left wondering how it was that a wanted man and his family could hide in plain sight for years. Home-owners on Evergreen Street and in the quiet community are too frightened to speak on camera, but at the same time suburban life goes on, and this quadruple murder is discounted from the daily national murder toll - about 16 a day in the Western Cape alone - as the victims and possibly the perpetrators were not local.



With the collapse of policing in general, and specifically a failure in the type of detailed and forensic policing required to challenge global organised crime head on, South Africa, with its mix of relatively good lifestyle and lawlessness, has become an attractive destination for crooks and charlatans from all over the world. In the past five years, members of Interpol’s office in Pretoria, have successfully arrested more than 60 fugitives wanted on extradition requests and Interpol Red Notices.



And it appears that members of the Bulgarian Mafia have put down roots here over the last decade and a half.



How do we know this? Every few years, they leave their tracks too obviously in the sand and make dramatic headlines. The assassination of Kamanev was disturbingly similar to another hit in 2018 when a Bulgarian national ANGELO DIMEV and his wife, NESSIE PEEVA, a speciality cake baker, and their child were assassinated, in their home in Bergvliet, a few kilometres away. At the time, DIMOV was out on bail for credit card fraud. He was represented by criminal lawyer WILLIAM BOOTH, a key defender of dodgy Bulgarians. DIMEV had a reputation as the “Ecstasy Guy” because he got get the drug so fast for whoever wanted it. He was also linked to money-laundering through strip clubs, and to a Bulgarian cocaine king-pin called “Taki”. After the murder, 930 Mandrax pills were allegedly found in the garden shed. No arrests for his murder were made.



Then in 2021, the South African police seized a ship, the Windward, as it docked in Saldanha Bay carrying almost a tonne of cocaine - 937 bricks - worth 580 million rands. It was the second largest cocaine seizure in South Africa’s history. Four Bulgarians and a crew from Myanmar were arrested on the boat. Altogether assets worth more than 46 million rand were seized from their houses of the suspects, some of which were in cash, but also vehicles and other assets. It was a coup for the police, but at the same time, it was understood that they had help from another large foreign intelligence agency who are moving in to prevent global mafia using South Africa as a transport hub to get cocaine to the lucrative market in Australia.



At least one of these convicted men - ASEN GEORGIEV IVANOV - had been picked up by the police before, some seven years earlier. IVANOV had been surprised by police while digging a hole in the garage of a house in an upmarket Durbanville Estate. A man in a Hazmat suit had been spotted walking around and there was a strong smell of sulphur - all leading police to believe that the garage was destined to be a drug lab hidden in a quiet suburb. The raid yielded millions of rands in cash found in rooms in the house and the house sale itself appeared to be suspect - purchased with diamonds from a melted down gold bracelet owned by a Slovakian woman, who had left the country. One of the other men in this bust may have been KRASIMIR KAMENOV’s business partner - his name is spelled slightly differently in company records as Kiril Slavchev Kirilov. The SAPS seized the cash - over R2,5 million - but the men got away and kept the property. That was all in 2014.



Back to the cocaine bust from the ship seized in Saldanha - this time IVANOV and two of his criminal friends were jailed for a collective 60 years in jail, despite being defended by the ubiquitous WILLIAM BOOTH. Significantly the men were found guilty not only of drug dealing but also of entering South Africa illegally using fake documents.



It’s the fake documents which are interesting - in the light of an extraordinarily big court case which simply disappeared. In July 2014 - the same year that Ivanov was digging up his garage floor to make a jacuzzi, Home Affairs and the police raided the office of immigration lawyer CRAIG SMITH and Associates after it was alleged that he was faking documents in order to get foreign nationals visas, work permits and residencies. Carte Blanche covered the raid and exposed CRAIG SMITH as selling work visas. After examining extensive files, the police charged CRAIG SMITH, his wife and his secretary in 2015 with over a thousand charges ranging from racketeering, incitement, fraud, forgery, uttering and money laundering. The charges arose from transactions between 2011 and 2014 and the state had 90 lever arch files full of evidence. The court papers said that much of the forgery was done by a Russian IT expert called NIKITA GIADOUK, in Smith's employ. Some reports say that CRAIG SMITH and Associates especially worked with Eastern Europeans - there was an affidavit that indicated that.



The Sunday Times reported on the affidavit as follows:

Capt Mark McLean said Smith allegedly had “Eastern European and other underworld connections.”

“The various witnesses have suggested that Smith fostered connections of the type described, by virtue of having done work for both Mavericks strip club, as well as Teasers strip club, which is allegedly owned by a Bulgarian,”said McLean in his affidavit.

“Smith allegedly assisted both of these businesses with permit application for their strippers, who were generally brought from Eastern European countries.



Eight years later, the case appears to have stalled. CRAIG SMITH and Associates are still practicing and Smith is often called as a commentator on immigration issues on radio and TV, as if there were no cloud over his head. NIKITA GIADOUK has moved to Venice where he has turned a loft apartment into an Airbnb and has put out on You Tube a tutorial on how foreigners can fill in an Italian visa. What seemed like a moment in 2015 to plug the hole in the leaky immigration dyke has passed.



The affidavit quoted in the Sunday Times points to another simmering Bulgarian presence in Cape Town - the owner of a strip club called STILLETOS, which appears to be the old TEAZERS. According to sources, JIFCO IVANOV was charged in 2015 with presenting faked documents for gun licences for two guns. And the case then disappeared as a result of bad policing. (The policeman who worked on the case is in retirement, and doesn’t want to talk.) JIFCO IVANOV appears to be some sort of kingpin who has avoided police detection. Apparently he has trafficked Eastern European girls who dance in his club, but there is no evidence to support that.



Which brings us back to KAMANEV - was he in the country legally? And was he mafia? Bulgarian investigative journalists say that he was part of a network of Bulgarian criminals called VIS-2, which acted as something of an insurance company for people who operated beyond the law. It has also been suggested that his murder may have been by mobsters because he was leaking to foreign intelligence agencies (possibly the FBI, sources suggest to me) to save his own skin. He was wanted by Interpol for murder and but also possible for his involvement in a cryptocurrency scam, One Coin. None of this is confirmed to date.



Meanwhile the European Union is postponing Bulgarian’s adoption of the euro, due to inflation, and significantly concerns about money-laundering and illegal immigration. Bulgaria is the EU’s poorest state. It operates a large, cash-based grey economy and has high levels of corruption and violence.



What we have today in Cape Town is a heap of dead Bulgarians, a tonne of cocaine, millions of cash seized by the state from Bulgarian nationals over time, and over a thousand charges against an immigration lawyer who is accused of forging documents….charges which have disappeared into thin air. It seems that despite some efforts at policing, Cape Town has been a great landing pad for Bulgaria’s worst export.

Press Release:


FOR YEARS KRASIMIR KAMENOV HAD A FEARSOME REPUTATION AS A MOBSTER ON THE STREETS OF BULGARIA. BUT FOR OVER A DECADE HE WAS HIDING OUT IN CONSTANTIA, LIVING THE HIGH LIFE WITH HIS BEAUTY QUEEN WIFE AND ENTOURAGE, SOCIALISING WITH OTHER EX-PATRIATE BULGARIANS IN CAPE TOWN. One of the last people to interview him was investigative journalist Aron Hymen SEEKING ANSWERS ON CREDIT CARD FRAUD SYNDICATES AND COCAINE SMUGGLING. Now Kamenov is dead, brutally assassinated with his FAMILY AND STAFF. THE MURDERS REMAIN A MYSTERY DESPITE AN ONGOING POLICE INVESTIGATION AND SPECULATION ACROSS NEWSROOMS OF MOB INFIGHTING AND CRYPTOCURRENCY SCAMS. IT’S UP TO JOURNALISTS AND THINKTANKS TO PIECE TOGETHER THE PUZZLE OF THE ORGANISED CRIMINAL NETWORKS PUTTING DOWN ROOTS IN AFRICA. EASTERN EUROPEAN CRIMINALS HAVE COME TO CAPE TOWN TO SET UP STATIONS FOR DRUG TRAFFICKING AND PRODUCTION, EXPLOITING THE COUNTRY’S UNPROTECTED COASTLINE, IT’S POROUS PORTS AND LACK-LUSTRE POLICING. AND MUCH OF THE EVIL FLOURISHES IN THE LEAFY LANES OF WELL-TO- DO SUBURBS WHERE NEIGHBOURS TURN A BLIND EYE TO THE COMINGS AND GOINGS OF GLAMOROUS FOREIGNERS.

MANY SOUTH AFRICAN DETECTIVES WHO WERE DEDICATED TO INVESTIGATING ORGANISED CRIME HAVE RETIRED, LEAVING THE COUNTRY EXPOSED TO GROUPS SETTING UP GLOBAL CRIMINAL TRADE ROUTES.
AND CAPE TOWN IS EN ROUTE TO EVERYWHERE.

ERIN BATES piece to cam: There's a regular stream of containers in and out of the entrance to Cape Town's port. They are evidence of the extent to which South Africa's harbours are trade hub for goods shipped all around the world: dry foods, fresh fruit and vegetables, wine, household and luxury goods - and when nobody's looking drugs and contraband

(VO) SHIPPING CONTAINERS ARE AN OBVIOUS CHOICE FOR SMUGGLERS, ACCORDING TO THE GLOBAL INITIATIVE AGAINST TRANSNATIONAL ORGANISED CRIME. RUGGERO SCATURRO ANALYSES HOW CONTRABAND TRAVELS GLOBALLY FROM SOURCE TO DESTINATION.

RUGGERO SCATTURO, analyst from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime (GI-TOC)
More than 80% of the world trade is shipped by containers
and according to the UNODC estimates,
only two to four percent of these containers are physically checked and inspected. Together with the extraordinary number of seizures of illicit drugs
found concealed in containers, of course, raised questions regarding the level of infiltration that drug traffickers have reached in the global supply chain via containerized cargo and of course, the opportunities that the latter offers at the many stages of the shipping routes.

(VO) KAMENOV’S MURDER AND THE 2021 COCAINE BUST HAVE ADDED TO THE INFORMATION ABOUT HOW SYNDICATES ARE OPERATING IN SOUTH AFRICA.

Zoom call
This somehow also gives an understanding of the extent of Bulgarians’ power in South Africa, also the possibility to rely on local networks and to move cocaine to and through South Africa in a relatively free manner.


(VO) IN THE COURSE OF OUR INVESTIGATION, ONE BULGARIAN NAME SURFACED: JIVKO LIBTCHEV IVANOV. HE’S BEEN IN BUSINESS IN SOUTH AFRICA FOR AT LEAST TWENTY YEARS.

HE OWNS STILETTO’s, A STRIP CLUB, IN DOWNTOWN CAPE TOWN. IT’S A DISTRICT NOTORIOUS FOR TURF WARS BETWEEN CRIME BOSSES AND THEIR CLUB BOUNCERS. IVANOV HAS HAD BRUSHES WITH THE LAW OVER TIME – BUT NO CONVICTIONS.

(VO) WE TRACKED HIM DOWN TO FIND OUT WHAT HE MADE OF THE STORY OF THE BULGARIAN MAFIA.

Summary: In South Africa life is cheap. Despite this, it’s an attractive destination for foreign criminals building global trade routes, who can exploit the Cape's rugged unprotected coastline and faltering police services for their own nefarious ends. On the 25th of May this year, a wet Thursday morning, four Bulgarian nationals were shot dead in their home in Constantia just after 08h00 am. The main target it appears was fifty-five-year-old KRASIMIR NIKOLAEV KAMENOV, a Bulgarian wanted by Interpol on behalf of the Bulgarian Police. But the assassins also took out his wife, their au pair and one of their two bodyguards, leaving three orphaned children. The South African Police moved swiftly to close up the broken entrance and comb the large house for clues, seizing ADT footage from the cameras that watch the street. It’s a high profile case which was scooped up by the Hawks, who have yet to formally identify the victims. Kamanev’s neighbours, who rarely saw him and the family, were left wondering how it was that a wanted man and his family could hide in plain sight for years. Home-owners on Evergreen Street and in the quiet community are too frightened to speak on camera, but at the same time suburban life goes on, and this quadruple murder is discounted from the daily national murder toll - about 16 a day in the Western Cape alone - as the victims and possibly the perpetrators were not local. With the collapse of policing in general, and specifically a failure in the type of detailed and forensic policing required to challenge global organised crime head on, South Africa, with its mix of relatively good lifestyle and lawlessness, has become an attractive destination for crooks and charlatans from all over the world. In the past five years, members of Interpol’s office in Pretoria, have successfully arrested more than 60 fugitives wanted on extradition requests and Interpol Red Notices. And it appears that members of the Bulgarian Mafia have put down roots here over the last decade and a half. How do we know this? Every few years, they leave their tracks too obviously in the sand and make dramatic headlines. The assassination of Kamanev was disturbingly similar to another hit in 2018 when a Bulgarian national ANGELO DIMEV and his wife, NESSIE PEEVA, a speciality cake baker, and their child were assassinated, in their home in Bergvliet, a few kilometres away. At the time, DIMOV was out on bail for credit card fraud. He was represented by criminal lawyer WILLIAM BOOTH, a key defender of dodgy Bulgarians. DIMEV had a reputation as the “Ecstasy Guy” because he got get the drug so fast for whoever wanted it. He was also linked to money-laundering through strip clubs, and to a Bulgarian cocaine king-pin called “Taki”. After the murder, 930 Mandrax pills were allegedly found in the garden shed. No arrests for his murder were made. Then in 2021, the South African police seized a ship, the Windward, as it docked in Saldanha Bay carrying almost a tonne of cocaine - 937 bricks - worth 580 million rands. It was the second largest cocaine seizure in South Africa’s history. Four Bulgarians and a crew from Myanmar were arrested on the boat. Altogether assets worth more than 46 million rand were seized from their houses of the suspects, some of which were in cash, but also vehicles and other assets. It was a coup for the police, but at the same time, it was understood that they had help from another large foreign intelligence agency who are moving in to prevent global mafia using South Africa as a transport hub to get cocaine to the lucrative market in Australia. At least one of these convicted men - ASEN GEORGIEV IVANOV - had been picked up by the police before, some seven years earlier. IVANOV had been surprised by police while digging a hole in the garage of a house in an upmarket Durbanville Estate. A man in a Hazmat suit had been spotted walking around and there was a strong smell of sulphur - all leading police to believe that the garage was destined to be a drug lab hidden in a quiet suburb. The raid yielded millions of rands in cash found in rooms in the house and the house sale itself appeared to be suspect - purchased with diamonds from a melted down gold bracelet owned by a Slovakian woman, who had left the country. One of the other men in this bust may have been KRASIMIR KAMENOV’s business partner - his name is spelled slightly differently in company records as Kiril Slavchev Kirilov. The SAPS seized the cash - over R2,5 million - but the men got away and kept the property. That was all in 2014. Back to the cocaine bust from the ship seized in Saldanha - this time IVANOV and two of his criminal friends were jailed for a collective 60 years in jail, despite being defended by the ubiquitous WILLIAM BOOTH. Significantly the men were found guilty not only of drug dealing but also of entering South Africa illegally using fake documents. It’s the fake documents which are interesting - in the light of an extraordinarily big court case which simply disappeared. In July 2014 - the same year that Ivanov was digging up his garage floor to make a jacuzzi, Home Affairs and the police raided the office of immigration lawyer CRAIG SMITH and Associates after it was alleged that he was faking documents in order to get foreign nationals visas, work permits and residencies. Carte Blanche covered the raid and exposed CRAIG SMITH as selling work visas. After examining extensive files, the police charged CRAIG SMITH, his wife and his secretary in 2015 with over a thousand charges ranging from racketeering, incitement, fraud, forgery, uttering and money laundering. The charges arose from transactions between 2011 and 2014 and the state had 90 lever arch files full of evidence. The court papers said that much of the forgery was done by a Russian IT expert called NIKITA GIADOUK, in Smith's employ. Some reports say that CRAIG SMITH and Associates especially worked with Eastern Europeans - there was an affidavit that indicated that. The Sunday Times reported on the affidavit as follows: Capt Mark McLean said Smith allegedly had “Eastern European and other underworld connections.” “The various witnesses have suggested that Smith fostered connections of the type described, by virtue of having done work for both Mavericks strip club, as well as Teasers strip club, which is allegedly owned by a Bulgarian,”said McLean in his affidavit. “Smith allegedly assisted both of these businesses with permit application for their strippers, who were generally brought from Eastern European countries. Eight years later, the case appears to have stalled. CRAIG SMITH and Associates are still practicing and Smith is often called as a commentator on immigration issues on radio and TV, as if there were no cloud over his head. NIKITA GIADOUK has moved to Venice where he has turned a loft apartment into an Airbnb and has put out on You Tube a tutorial on how foreigners can fill in an Italian visa. What seemed like a moment in 2015 to plug the hole in the leaky immigration dyke has passed. The affidavit quoted in the Sunday Times points to another simmering Bulgarian presence in Cape Town - the owner of a strip club called STILLETOS, which appears to be the old TEAZERS. According to sources, JIFCO IVANOV was charged in 2015 with presenting faked documents for gun licences for two guns. And the case then disappeared as a result of bad policing. (The policeman who worked on the case is in retirement, and doesn’t want to talk.) JIFCO IVANOV appears to be some sort of kingpin who has avoided police detection. Apparently he has trafficked Eastern European girls who dance in his club, but there is no evidence to support that. Which brings us back to KAMANEV - was he in the country legally? And was he mafia? Bulgarian investigative journalists say that he was part of a network of Bulgarian criminals called VIS-2, which acted as something of an insurance company for people who operated beyond the law. It has also been suggested that his murder may have been by mobsters because he was leaking to foreign intelligence agencies (possibly the FBI, sources suggest to me) to save his own skin. He was wanted by Interpol for murder and but also possible for his involvement in a cryptocurrency scam, One Coin. None of this is confirmed to date. Meanwhile the European Union is postponing Bulgarian’s adoption of the euro, due to inflation, and significantly concerns about money-laundering and illegal immigration. Bulgaria is the EU’s poorest state. It operates a large, cash-based grey economy and has high levels of corruption and violence. What we have today in Cape Town is a heap of dead Bulgarians, a tonne of cocaine, millions of cash seized by the state from Bulgarian nationals over time, and over a thousand charges against an immigration lawyer who is accused of forging documents….charges which have disappeared into thin air. It seems that despite some efforts at policing, Cape Town has been a great landing pad for Bulgaria’s worst export. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight we reveal how the Bulgarian Mafia put down it's roots in Cape Town creating criminal networks which have led to drug smuggling, human trafficking and murders...neither friend or enemy are spar
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The murder of four Bulgarian nationals in Constantia on May 25th gives us a hook on which to build the complex story of the Bulgarian Mafia in Cape Town and how poor policing, dodgy immigration lawyers and an unprotected coastline facilitated the flourishing of a violent criminal group, often in the shadows of quiet suburbs.
metadata.Summary: In South Africa life is cheap. Despite this, it’s an attractive destination for foreign criminals building global trade routes, who can exploit the Cape's rugged unprotected coastline and faltering police services for their own nefarious ends. On the 25th of May this year, a wet Thursday morning, four Bulgarian nationals were shot dead in their home in Constantia just after 08h00 am. The main target it appears was fifty-five-year-old KRASIMIR NIKOLAEV KAMENOV, a Bulgarian wanted by Interpol on behalf of the Bulgarian Police. But the assassins also took out his wife, their au pair and one of their two bodyguards, leaving three orphaned children. The South African Police moved swiftly to close up the broken entrance and comb the large house for clues, seizing ADT footage from the cameras that watch the street. It’s a high profile case which was scooped up by the Hawks, who have yet to formally identify the victims. Kamanev’s neighbours, who rarely saw him and the family, were left wondering how it was that a wanted man and his family could hide in plain sight for years. Home-owners on Evergreen Street and in the quiet community are too frightened to speak on camera, but at the same time suburban life goes on, and this quadruple murder is discounted from the daily national murder toll - about 16 a day in the Western Cape alone - as the victims and possibly the perpetrators were not local. With the collapse of policing in general, and specifically a failure in the type of detailed and forensic policing required to challenge global organised crime head on, South Africa, with its mix of relatively good lifestyle and lawlessness, has become an attractive destination for crooks and charlatans from all over the world. In the past five years, members of Interpol’s office in Pretoria, have successfully arrested more than 60 fugitives wanted on extradition requests and Interpol Red Notices. And it appears that members of the Bulgarian Mafia have put down roots here over the last decade and a half. How do we know this? Every few years, they leave their tracks too obviously in the sand and make dramatic headlines. The assassination of Kamanev was disturbingly similar to another hit in 2018 when a Bulgarian national ANGELO DIMEV and his wife, NESSIE PEEVA, a speciality cake baker, and their child were assassinated, in their home in Bergvliet, a few kilometres away. At the time, DIMOV was out on bail for credit card fraud. He was represented by criminal lawyer WILLIAM BOOTH, a key defender of dodgy Bulgarians. DIMEV had a reputation as the “Ecstasy Guy” because he got get the drug so fast for whoever wanted it. He was also linked to money-laundering through strip clubs, and to a Bulgarian cocaine king-pin called “Taki”. After the murder, 930 Mandrax pills were allegedly found in the garden shed. No arrests for his murder were made. Then in 2021, the South African police seized a ship, the Windward, as it docked in Saldanha Bay carrying almost a tonne of cocaine - 937 bricks - worth 580 million rands. It was the second largest cocaine seizure in South Africa’s history. Four Bulgarians and a crew from Myanmar were arrested on the boat. Altogether assets worth more than 46 million rand were seized from their houses of the suspects, some of which were in cash, but also vehicles and other assets. It was a coup for the police, but at the same time, it was understood that they had help from another large foreign intelligence agency who are moving in to prevent global mafia using South Africa as a transport hub to get cocaine to the lucrative market in Australia. At least one of these convicted men - ASEN GEORGIEV IVANOV - had been picked up by the police before, some seven years earlier. IVANOV had been surprised by police while digging a hole in the garage of a house in an upmarket Durbanville Estate. A man in a Hazmat suit had been spotted walking around and there was a strong smell of sulphur - all leading police to believe that the garage was destined to be a drug lab hidden in a quiet suburb. The raid yielded millions of rands in cash found in rooms in the house and the house sale itself appeared to be suspect - purchased with diamonds from a melted down gold bracelet owned by a Slovakian woman, who had left the country. One of the other men in this bust may have been KRASIMIR KAMENOV’s business partner - his name is spelled slightly differently in company records as Kiril Slavchev Kirilov. The SAPS seized the cash - over R2,5 million - but the men got away and kept the property. That was all in 2014. Back to the cocaine bust from the ship seized in Saldanha - this time IVANOV and two of his criminal friends were jailed for a collective 60 years in jail, despite being defended by the ubiquitous WILLIAM BOOTH. Significantly the men were found guilty not only of drug dealing but also of entering South Africa illegally using fake documents. It’s the fake documents which are interesting - in the light of an extraordinarily big court case which simply disappeared. In July 2014 - the same year that Ivanov was digging up his garage floor to make a jacuzzi, Home Affairs and the police raided the office of immigration lawyer CRAIG SMITH and Associates after it was alleged that he was faking documents in order to get foreign nationals visas, work permits and residencies. Carte Blanche covered the raid and exposed CRAIG SMITH as selling work visas. After examining extensive files, the police charged CRAIG SMITH, his wife and his secretary in 2015 with over a thousand charges ranging from racketeering, incitement, fraud, forgery, uttering and money laundering. The charges arose from transactions between 2011 and 2014 and the state had 90 lever arch files full of evidence. The court papers said that much of the forgery was done by a Russian IT expert called NIKITA GIADOUK, in Smith's employ. Some reports say that CRAIG SMITH and Associates especially worked with Eastern Europeans - there was an affidavit that indicated that. The Sunday Times reported on the affidavit as follows: Capt Mark McLean said Smith allegedly had “Eastern European and other underworld connections.” “The various witnesses have suggested that Smith fostered connections of the type described, by virtue of having done work for both Mavericks strip club, as well as Teasers strip club, which is allegedly owned by a Bulgarian,”said McLean in his affidavit. “Smith allegedly assisted both of these businesses with permit application for their strippers, who were generally brought from Eastern European countries. Eight years later, the case appears to have stalled. CRAIG SMITH and Associates are still practicing and Smith is often called as a commentator on immigration issues on radio and TV, as if there were no cloud over his head. NIKITA GIADOUK has moved to Venice where he has turned a loft apartment into an Airbnb and has put out on You Tube a tutorial on how foreigners can fill in an Italian visa. What seemed like a moment in 2015 to plug the hole in the leaky immigration dyke has passed. The affidavit quoted in the Sunday Times points to another simmering Bulgarian presence in Cape Town - the owner of a strip club called STILLETOS, which appears to be the old TEAZERS. According to sources, JIFCO IVANOV was charged in 2015 with presenting faked documents for gun licences for two guns. And the case then disappeared as a result of bad policing. (The policeman who worked on the case is in retirement, and doesn’t want to talk.) JIFCO IVANOV appears to be some sort of kingpin who has avoided police detection. Apparently he has trafficked Eastern European girls who dance in his club, but there is no evidence to support that. Which brings us back to KAMANEV - was he in the country legally? And was he mafia? Bulgarian investigative journalists say that he was part of a network of Bulgarian criminals called VIS-2, which acted as something of an insurance company for people who operated beyond the law. It has also been suggested that his murder may have been by mobsters because he was leaking to foreign intelligence agencies (possibly the FBI, sources suggest to me) to save his own skin. He was wanted by Interpol for murder and but also possible for his involvement in a cryptocurrency scam, One Coin. None of this is confirmed to date. Meanwhile the European Union is postponing Bulgarian’s adoption of the euro, due to inflation, and significantly concerns about money-laundering and illegal immigration. Bulgaria is the EU’s poorest state. It operates a large, cash-based grey economy and has high levels of corruption and violence. What we have today in Cape Town is a heap of dead Bulgarians, a tonne of cocaine, millions of cash seized by the state from Bulgarian nationals over time, and over a thousand charges against an immigration lawyer who is accused of forging documents….charges which have disappeared into thin air. It seems that despite some efforts at policing, Cape Town has been a great landing pad for Bulgaria’s worst export.
